title: Following the Cash: Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion & Balance Sheet
web_title: 6. Following the Cash: Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion & Balance Sheet
book_title: Chapter 6: Following the Cash: Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion & Balance Sheet
question: Is the profit turning into cash, and can the balance sheet carry the growth?

epigraph.quote: “We recognise that sustainable growth requires financial discipline, operational excellence and the ability to convert earnings into healthy cash flows over time.”
epigraph.author: D. P. Jhawar, MD & CEO, ProV H1 FY27 shareholders’ letter, 13 November 2026

web_blocks.title: The long arc: revenue, profit and sources

web_blocks.html: FY2020–FY2022 come from the restated prospectus [10]; FY2023–FY2026 from audited annual reports [16][15][14][3]. H1 FY27 is unaudited, limited-reviewed and filed as scanned images, so its line items carry about ₹1 lakh of tolerance [1]. Screener tables are rounded [67].

web_blocks.caption: Consolidated long arc, ₹ crore
web_blocks.takeaway: FY21–FY22 cash flow and FY23–FY24 borrowings are rounded Screener values.

web_blocks.html: The FY2020 loss came when over half of revenue was bulk commodity trading; the prospectus attributes it mainly to ₹19.26 crore of derivative trading losses during the Covid lockdown, plus a large stock build and ₹11.24 crore of finance cost [10]. From FY2021 revenue compounded at 25.2% to FY2026, and PAT at 57% over FY2023–FY2026, yet PAT margin only moved from 0.9% to 1.5%.

web_blocks.caption: Profit and loss, Screener consolidated FY2021–FY2026
web_blocks.takeaway: Revenue tripled and net profit grew about sevenfold, while operating margin stayed near 1–2% and tax near 20%.

web_blocks.html: Operating profit rose from ₹3 Cr to ₹19 Cr with other income only ₹1 Cr in FY2026, so profit growth is operating.

web_blocks.title: The margin bridge: where each gross-margin point went

web_blocks.html: Reported gross margin is revenue less materials, purchases and stock change in the filed statements. Employee and other expenses then show how much reaches EBITDA.

Gross margin rose 266 bps from FY2023 to FY2026, but other expenses rose 229 bps, so EBITDA excluding other income gained only 48 bps. In H1 FY27 gross margin gained 149 bps on H1 FY26, expenses took 125 bps, and EBITDA gained 24 bps. About 85% of each gross-margin point is reinvested; part of the employee-cost rise is contract staff moved onto payroll [2].

web_blocks.caption: Management metrics against filed statements
rows: Implied brand profit exceeds total; basis differs
₹20.21 Cr expense line; ₹4.55 Cr in FY2025 [3]
About ₹55 Cr not visible; likely netted against revenue (our inference)
web_blocks.takeaway: FY2026 deck and annual report against audited statements.

web_blocks.html: These gaps do not show misstatement. Management’s brand economics cannot be rebuilt from audited lines, so we rely on reported margin and treat management figures, including its 61-day working-capital cycle, as direction.

web_blocks.title: Balance sheet, debt and the ₹21 Cr of liquid funds

web_blocks.html: Net cash was about ₹19.6 Cr at 31 March 2026: ₹25.5 Cr of cash plus ₹21.1 Cr of liquid funds less ₹27.0 Cr of borrowings [3].

web_blocks.caption: Balance sheet, Screener consolidated FY2021–FY2026
web_blocks.takeaway: Reserves grew from ₹49 Cr to ₹141 Cr; borrowings fell to ₹2 Cr in FY2024 and rebuilt to ₹27 Cr.

web_blocks.html: The ₹21 Cr of investments were three quoted liquid funds, redeemed in H1 FY27, while Surat sat in work in progress (₹10.2 Cr) [3][1].

web_blocks.caption: Balance sheet movement in H1 FY27, ₹ crore
web_blocks.takeaway: Consolidated balance sheets [3][1]; net debt is our arithmetic.

web_blocks.html: Working-capital assets grew about ₹95 Cr in six months; payables financed ₹15 Cr, cash and liquid funds fell ₹41 Cr, and debt rose ₹29 Cr. Finance cost rose from ₹0.21 Cr to ₹0.90 Cr [1]. ICICI Bank lends at about 9.15% for working capital and 9.30% for the Surat term loan, secured on the property and a director’s flat, with personal and parent guarantees. Contingent liabilities are ₹0.81 Cr, and the parent’s ₹14.86 Cr loan to Prov Foods is eliminated on consolidation [3].

web_blocks.title: Following the cash: why operating cash flow lagged profit

web_blocks.html: Operating cash flow was negative in FY2023–FY2025, positive in FY2026 and negative in H1 FY27. Cumulative FY2023–FY2026 CFO was about ₹0.7 Cr against PAT of ₹32.5 Cr, before ₹6.9 Cr of interest [16][15][14][3].

web_blocks.caption: Cash flow, Screener consolidated FY2021–FY2026
web_blocks.takeaway: Operating cash flow was at or below zero in five of six years while profit rose every year.

web_blocks.html: Free cash flow was negative from FY2021 to FY2025 on Screener’s definition; the IPO and later debt paid for the gap. The next table shows which line absorbed cash.

web_blocks.caption: Operating cash flow reconciliation, ₹ crore
web_blocks.takeaway: Audited cash-flow statements [16][15][14][3][1]; FY26 uses the audited ₹905.59 lakh, not the ₹883.11 lakh restated in the H1 filing.

web_blocks.html: The culprit changes yearly: receivables in FY2023, advances in FY2024, inventory in FY2025. FY2026 turned positive because payables released ₹8.2 Cr and debtor days fell from 23 to 15. Over four years ₹54 Cr went into inventory, receivables and advances against ₹10 Cr from payables. Of ₹31.5 Cr of March 2026 advances, ₹19.1 Cr went to suppliers [3].

The cycle is seasonal: H2 FY26 produced about ₹43 Cr after H1’s build. But H1 FY27 absorbed ₹23.5 Cr more than H1 FY26, mostly in inventory and supplier advances. One digit of the scanned H1 FY27 inventory line is smudged; we use ₹28.9 Cr because it matches the printed subtotal and the balance sheet, where ₹23.9 Cr would not.

web_blocks.title: Working capital, days and a sustainable growth rate

web_blocks.html: Screener shows cash conversion improving through FY2026.

web_blocks.caption: Working-capital days and ROCE, Screener consolidated FY2021–FY2026
web_blocks.takeaway: Since FY2023 debtor days fell from 31 to 15 and the cash cycle from 46 to 31 days, while ROCE reached only 12% in FY2026.

web_blocks.html: March figures flatter the position. On a half-year basis (our calculation), debtor days rose from about 13 to 23, inventory days from 22 to 29, and the cash cycle from 27 to 39 days by September. We reconstruct working capital at about ₹97 Cr (16.7% of revenue) in March 2025, ₹107 Cr (11.6%) in March 2026 and ₹187 Cr in September 2026 (16.0% of trailing revenue). FY2026’s cash came from that five-point drop, unlikely to repeat.

web_blocks.the_number: Growth funded from the business’s own cash earnings is about 14% a year (range 10–17%). At about ₹1,300 Cr of FY2027 revenue, operating cash flow before capex would be about −₹25 Cr (range −₹14 Cr to −₹35 Cr).
web_blocks.how_calculated: Self-funded growth equals cash-earnings margin divided by working capital as a share of revenue. Margin is PAT plus depreciation: 1.68% in FY2026, 2.0% in H1 FY27. Working capital is 11.6% of revenue at March 2026 and 16.0% of trailing revenue at September. The four pairings span 10.5% to 17.2%, averaging about 14%. With H2 FY27 revenue 25% above H2 FY2026, FY2027 is about ₹1,300 Cr. That needs ₹43–60 Cr of extra working capital against cash earnings of ₹22–26 Cr plus ₹3 Cr of non-cash deferred tax.
web_blocks.the_inputs: Revenue ₹925.0 Cr FY2026, ₹633.3 Cr H1 FY27, ₹535.4 Cr H2 FY2026; extra FY2027 revenue ₹375 Cr; PAT plus depreciation ₹15.5 Cr and ₹12.6 Cr; working capital (inventory, receivables, advances less payables) ₹107.1 Cr and ₹186.7 Cr [3][1].
web_blocks.the_range: Self-funded growth 10–17%; FY2027 operating cash flow before capex between −₹14 Cr and −₹35 Cr, before Surat Phases 2 and 3.
web_blocks.if_off: If working capital returns toward 12% of revenue, FY2027 cash flow could be near zero. At 16% with growth near 29%, debt or equity must fund roughly ₹30–35 Cr a year.

web_blocks.html: Against a brand-growth guide near 29%, growth consumes more cash than the business earns unless working capital shrinks.

web_blocks.title: Earnings quality, tax, returns and dilution

web_blocks.html: Other income was 41% of FY2024 EBITDA on management’s definition, 21% in FY2025, 7% in FY2026 and 4% in H1 FY27. FY2024 included ₹3.68 Cr of derivative trading profit and FY2026 none; no hedging policy is disclosed [16][15][14][3]. Falling other income improves quality. Tax is booked near 20%, but 38% of the FY2026 charge was deferred and cash tax was 9.9% of pre-tax profit. Deferred tax assets fell from ₹3.8 Cr to ₹1.7 Cr in a year [1].

Screener shows ROCE of 12% for FY2026; the annual report gives ROE of 9.88% [67][3]. Our ROE of 10.3% divides parent PAT of ₹14.14 Cr by average net worth of ₹137.2 Cr; ROCE of 11.5% divides EBIT of ₹18.59 Cr by average capital employed of ₹161.8 Cr. From FY2023 to FY2026 capital employed rose about ₹84 Cr, much of it IPO equity, while EBIT rose ₹11.5 Cr: a 13.7% incremental pre-tax return, near the 9.2% cost of debt. Shares number 34.53 lakh, with 9,075 ESOP options and no dividend [3][21][31].

web_blocks.title: Genuine compounding versus accounting optics
paragraphs: Genuine: operating profit growth, normal taxes, audited gross margin gains, fading other income. Optics: management margin and marketing figures, March net cash at a seasonal high, and FY2026’s CFO from a one-time working-capital squeeze.

web_blocks.html: The evidence shows a growing, cleaner-earning business with modest returns, not yet a self-funding one. Unproven: normalised cash conversion, true brand margin, and Surat’s return on capex.

book_paragraphs: Let me tell you the oldest rule in my trade. Profit is an opinion; cash is a fact. You and I are going to apply it to Proventus now, and the exercise will be uncomfortable in places, because the income statement is a story of success and the cash-flow statement is a story of effort.

Start at the beginning. In FY2020 this company sold almost ₹900 crore of goods, over half of it bulk commodities, and lost ₹21.9 crore. Then it shrank deliberately. Revenue fell to about ₹300 crore and the business became marginally profitable. From that base it grew to ₹925 crore by FY2026, a compound rate of about twenty-five per cent. Profit after tax grew faster, from ₹3.7 crore in FY2023 to ₹14.3 crore in FY2026. Impressive. But look at the margin: about one and a half paise on every rupee. A shopkeeper who keeps one and a half paise has no room for mistakes.

So where do the margin points go? Here is the bridge in plain words. Between FY2023 and FY2026, the gross margin in the audited statements rose from 7.2% to 9.9%, a gain of 266 basis points. Other expenses, which is where marketing, freight and trade schemes live, rose 229 basis points. Staff costs fell slightly. So only about 48 basis points reached the bottom, and the first half of this year shows the same shape: a 149-point gain in gross margin, nearly all of it spent. Roughly eighty-five per cent of every margin point is being reinvested. Management calls that building a brand. A skeptic calls it running to stand still. Both are describing the same arithmetic.

Do you remember the management gross margin of 23%? Place it beside the audited ledger. Twenty-three per cent of the half-year’s brand revenue is about ₹105 crore, but the filed accounts show gross profit of about ₹76 crore for the whole company in that half-year. The same gap shows up in marketing: ₹75 crore described in the deck, ₹20 crore visible as an expense line. I do not read that as hidden money. I read it as a measuring stick I cannot see. Where the ruler is not visible, I use the one I can see.

Now the cash. Walk with me through four years. In FY2023 customers owed the company ₹16 crore more, so cash went there. In FY2024 advances to suppliers and others rose about ₹15 crore. In FY2025 the warehouse filled with ₹16 crore of extra stock. In FY2026, at last, operating cash flow turned positive, by about ₹9 crore. Add the four years and you get ₹0.7 crore of operating cash against ₹32.5 crore of profit. Where did the other ₹32 crore go? Into stock, into receivables, into advances to suppliers. The profit is real. It simply lives in a warehouse and on a customer’s ledger.

And what of the good year? FY2026’s positive cash did not come from earning more per rupee of sales. It came from the working-capital burden falling from about 16.7% of revenue to 11.6%, with debtor days dropping from 23 to 15 and payables releasing cash. You can do that once. You cannot do it every year.

Then came the six months to September. Receivables doubled, from ₹39 crore to ₹79 crore. Inventory rose ₹29 crore. Advances rose ₹26 crore. Operating cash flow was minus ₹57.6 crore. The company that had ₹19.6 crore of net cash in March was ₹51 crore in net debt by September. Part of this is seasonal: Diwali stock must be built before it is sold, and the same pattern gave minus ₹34 crore last year, followed by plus ₹43 crore in the second half. Fair enough. But this year’s build was ₹23 crore larger. Was that stocking the channel, or stuck money? I do not know, and the filing does not tell us.

One honest caution about those numbers. The half-year results were filed as scanned images, and one digit in the inventory line is smudged. I read it as ₹28.9 crore because that is the figure that makes the printed subtotal and the balance sheet agree. Small matter, but when I tell you what I know, I should tell you how I know it.

Picture the funding behind all this. A single bank, ICICI, supplies the working capital at about nine and a quarter per cent. The Surat term loan is secured on the factory, a flat owned by a director, and the personal guarantees of directors, with a guarantee from the parent on top. The parent has also lent its subsidiary nearly ₹15 crore of the IPO money, still outstanding. None of that is improper, and the contingent liabilities are under a crore. But it tells you who stands behind the growth: the promoters’ signatures, one lender and the subsidiary’s patience.

Let me give you my own estimate, labelled as judgment. If cash earnings are about two per cent of sales and working capital is between 11.6% and 16% of sales, the business can fund roughly fourteen per cent growth a year from its own pocket, in a range of ten to seventeen. Management is aiming for something near twenty-nine per cent in brand revenue. That means the gap must be borrowed. On my numbers, FY2027 operating cash flow before capex lands near minus ₹25 crore, within a range of minus ₹14 to minus ₹35 crore. If that sounds harsh, remember what growth is: the thing that eats the cash.

What about the quality of the profit itself? There is some good news. In FY2024, forty-one per cent of EBITDA was other income, including derivative trading profits. By this half-year it is four per cent. The profit now comes from selling goods, which is what you want. Tax is the other quiet thing. Only about ten per cent of pre-tax profit was paid in cash last year, because old losses were being used. That cushion is nearly gone, so cash tax will rise toward the book rate.

On returns, I find a company that is fine and not yet great. Return on capital of 11.5% and return on equity of about ten per cent, on my arithmetic. The extra capital added since FY2023 earned about 13.7% before tax, only a little above what the bank charges. Dividends: none. Share count: 34.5 lakh, with ESOP too small to matter. So the owner’s return comes from growth alone, and growth is the thing that needs the money.

So what would I watch if I were sitting at your desk? First, March receivables and inventory. If they settle back toward ₹40 crore and ₹60 crore while sales stay at the higher level, the September build was goods in motion. If they do not, it was money stuck. Second, supplier advances: ₹19 crore sat with suppliers at the last March, and advance payments are a quiet place for a profit to hide. Third, the gap between book tax and cash tax, which is about to close. And fourth, the first full year in which operating cash flow is positive without a one-off squeeze on payables. Four checks, none of them clever. They are simply the questions the numbers have not yet answered.

What do I conclude? The accounting is clean enough: unmodified opinions, a small contingent liability, and no derivative trading profit in FY2026. What is unproven is the conversion of profit into cash on a repeatable basis. In the CEO’s own November words, sustainable growth requires “the ability to convert earnings into healthy cash flows over time”. I could not have put it better. Until the cash catches up with the profit, I treat the profit as promising rather than proven.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: A growing company can run out of cash while reporting record profits, and the more it grows the faster that can happen. ProV’s four-year record is exactly that shape: ₹32.5 crore of profit, ₹0.7 crore of cash. The honest question for you is not whether the profit is real, but who is lending the working capital while the brand matures, and for how long they will keep doing it.
